subject: air-combat
title: Basic Fighter Maneuvers
objective: Understand one-versus-one BFM geometry, pursuit, turn performance, vertical maneuvering, energy and guns employment well enough to describe what each aircraft is doing and why.
applicability: Aircraft-agnostic concepts illustrated with US Navy T-45C training figures; type-specific numbers belong to that training example.

subject: airfield-operations
title: The Airfield and the Traffic Pattern
objective: Read a military airfield's runway numbers, markings, arresting gear, signs and lighting, read the PAPI and the Navy optical landing system, choose the runway in use from the wind, fly the overhead and the standard pattern, know where helicopters fly, make military field calls, and move safely on the ground.
applicability: Military pilots of all US services first: Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps and Army airfield practice, with shared US (FAA) standards and civil towered and non-towered procedures as supplementary. Each military field's course rules and published procedures take precedence.

subject: radio-communications
title: Radio Procedures and Phraseology
objective: Speak and understand military air–ground radio: multi-service brevity words, a training sortie's calls, call signs and preset channels, formation check-ins and training-rule calls, then the FAA technique, phonetic alphabet and numbers, contact calls, readbacks, emergency calls, transponder codes and what to do when the radio fails.
applicability: For US military pilots of all services: the joint Army, Marine Corps, Navy and Air Force brevity codes and a worked Navy training sortie first, with the FAA Aeronautical Information Manual as the supplementary US civil rule set; units and other countries differ in detail.

subject: flight-fundamentals
title: Fixed-Wing Principles of Flight
objective: Understand the four forces, lift and angle of attack, drag, control and stability, turns and load factor, stalls, the maneuvering envelope and energy well enough to explain what a military jet is doing and why.
applicability: For military pilots of every service: fixed-wing principles from Navy aerodynamics texts and its T-45 jet syllabus, with FAA handbooks as supplementary sources; worked numbers use an invented jet trainer, with US Navy T-45 training figures where cited.

subject: flight-fundamentals
title: Rotor-Wing Principles of Flight
objective: Understand how a helicopter's rotor makes lift and is controlled, from the blade's own relative wind, the collective, cyclic and pedals and the rotor systems to hover power, forward flight and dissymmetry of lift, then its hazards (retreating blade stall, vortex ring state, dynamic rollover, low G, low rotor rpm, loss of tail rotor effectiveness) and autorotation, well enough to explain what the rotor is doing and why.
applicability: For military helicopter pilots of every service: the Navy's Aerodynamics for Naval Aviators and the Army's Fundamentals of Flight first, with the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook as the supplementary source for most hazards; worked numbers use an invented utility helicopter. The type's operator's manual or NATOPS governs.

subject: navigation
title: Air Navigation
objective: Read the HSI as a picture, set up and fly a TACAN or VOR course, correct for wind, intercept courses inbound and outbound, fly DME arcs, point to point and waypoint routes, and cross-check them, with positions, headings and the navigation aids as background.
applicability: For military pilots of every service: US Navy training publications first, with the FAA AIM and Pilot's Handbook as the supplementary US civil rule set and an Army field manual for the military grid. Worked examples use the T-45C training jet's displays; your aircraft's flight manual (NATOPS or your service's equivalent) governs its systems.

subject: instrument-flight
title: Attitude Instrument Flying
objective: Fly the aircraft on instruments alone: read a panel as control and performance instruments, set attitude and power and let the lagging performance instruments catch up, fly a hub-and-spoke crosscheck without fixation or omission, recognize the illusions of spatial disorientation, and verify and recover from unusual attitudes, fixed- or rotary-wing, with or without an attitude indicator.
applicability: For military pilots of every service, fixed- and rotary-wing: the Air Force instrument flight procedures manual and the Navy's instrument training instructions, as generic technique, with the FAA Aeronautical Information Manual as the supplementary source for illusions. The figures use a generic panel and an invented flight model. Your service's instrument rules and the aircraft's flight manual govern.

subject: instrument-flight
title: Instrument Procedures
objective: Fly an instrument sortie: the departure climb, holding and its entries, the approach to minimums, the ILS and how its needles behave, PAR and ASR radar approaches, the missed approach, high-altitude penetrations, reading the approach plate and lost communications.
applicability: For military pilots of every service, fixed- and rotary-wing: the Air Force instrument flight procedures manual and the Navy's instrument training instructions first, as generic procedure, with the FAA Aeronautical Information Manual as the supplementary US rule set. Army instrument publications could not be read for this revision; your service's instrument rules, the aircraft's flight manual and current flight information publications govern.

subject: formation-flying
title: Two-Ship Formation
objective: Fly as a section: know the parade, cruise, combat cruise and combat spread positions, hold parade by its checkpoints in altitude, bearing, closure order, make the flight's check-ins and frequency changes, fly the breakup and rendezvous and recover from an underrun, run the lost sight and blind procedures, use the lead's lights at night, and recognise the tactical turns.
applicability: For military pilots of every service: the Navy training command's T-6B and T-44C formation material as generic technique, with type numbers as examples and the FAA's lighting rule as a supplement. Air Force and Army formation publications and helicopter formations are not yet covered; your service's formation rules, unit procedures and the aircraft's flight manual govern.

subject: air-to-ground-operations
title: Weapons Delivery
objective: Understand how an unguided weapon is delivered: the level, dive, loft and pop-up attacks and when each is used, the bombing triangle and the sight, release parameters and what an error in each does to the hit, bombing tables, low- and high-drag weapons, fuze arming and fragmentation, computed and manual sights, and the offset pop-up attack from the run-in to the recovery.
applicability: For military pilots of every service flying fixed-wing attack: the US Navy's T-45 weapons and operational navigation training instructions first, with sim manuals (DCS) for computed modes. Worked numbers are T-45 training-pattern numbers with practice bombs; your aircraft's tactical manual and your unit's rules govern.

subject: air-to-ground-operations
title: Close Air Support
objective: Understand how a close air support attack is controlled and briefed: who the JTAC and FAC(A) are and who controls what, Types 1, 2 and 3 control and the bomb-on-target and bomb-on-coordinate methods of attack, the check-in, game plan and 9-line brief line by line with its readbacks, correlation, marks and talk-ons, the clearance calls, and how danger close, friendly marking and attack headings prevent fratricide, for fixed- and rotary-wing aircraft of every service.
applicability: For military aircrew of every service who fly close air support, fixed- or rotary-wing: the joint close air support publication, which all four services follow, with Marine Corps attack helicopter CAS and Army close combat attack as that publication describes them. Worked briefs are invented examples in its formats; theater special instructions, your unit's procedures and the current edition govern.

subject: naval-operations
title: Carrier and Amphibious Ship Operations
objective: Understand how aircraft operate from ships: the carrier's flight deck, catapults and arresting gear, who wears which jersey, the launch, Case I, II and III recoveries, the Case I pattern, the lens and the ball, LSO calls and grades, bolters, waveoffs, tanking and bingo, then amphibious assault ship operations for helicopters, tiltrotors and the AV-8B, and Army deck landing qualification.
applicability: For military pilots of every service who fly from or train on ships: Navy and Marine Corps carrier aviation from Navy training publications, Navy and Marine Corps amphibious ship procedures from the Navy's air traffic control manual, and Army helicopter shipboard operations from the Army's own field manual. Worked numbers are T-45 carrier qualification numbers; the ship's and the aircraft's NATOPS or service manuals govern.
